title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Packages and data

library(tidyverse)   # includes ggplot2
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")


ggplot2 is part of the tidyverse. We’ll use the Palmer penguins data from week 4.


Warnings are switched off for this deck. Live, ggplot will print “Removed 2 rows containing missing values” — point it out once: two penguins have no measurements, and ggplot drops them rather than failing.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Components, not chart types
Instead of choosing “a scatter plot” or “a bar chart”, we describe a plot by its parts:


Data — a tidy tibble
Aesthetics (aes) — which variables control position, colour, size, …
Geometries (geom_*) — what is drawn: points, lines, bars, …



…plus optional stats, scales, coordinates and facets.


The payoff: the same handful of pieces builds every chart, so you learn one system rather than a menu of chart functions. Details of every component are in the notes.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Step 1: data and aesthetics






ImportantTask



Set up a plot of flipper length (x) against body mass (y). What do you see?




ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g))










Axes, but no data: we’ve said what to map, not how to draw it.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Step 2: add a geometry






ImportantTask



Draw one point per penguin.




ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point()










Layers are added with +.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
+, not |>






ImportantTask



What’s wrong with this code?



penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) |>
  geom_point()

Error in `geom_point()`:
! `mapping` must be created by `aes()`.
✖ You've supplied a <ggplot2::ggplot> object.
ℹ Did you use `%>%` or `|>` instead of `+`?




penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point()



Pipe the data in with |>; join layers with +. ggplot2 is older than the pipe — mixing them up is the most common beginner error.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Step 3: more aesthetics






ImportantTask



Colour the points by species.




ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g,
                     colour = species)) +
  geom_point()










A third variable, mapped to colour. size, shape and alpha (transparency) work the same way.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Step 4: labels and theme






ImportantTask



Give the plot a title, axis labels with units, and a cleaner look.




ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g,
                     colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Penguin flipper length vs body mass",
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    colour = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










Emphasise units in axis labels — this comes up again in the checklist at the end.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Facets






ImportantTask



Draw a separate panel for each island.




ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g,
                     colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~island) +
  theme_minimal()










Faceting splits the data into subsets with shared axes — ideal for comparing groups side by side.


Ask what the panels reveal: Gentoo only live on Biscoe; Chinstrap only on Dream; Adelie on all three. That’s a finding the single plot hid.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Layering geometries






ImportantTask



Add a straight-line trend for each species on top of the points.




ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g,
                     colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_minimal()










geom_smooth() applies a statistical transformation (here a linear fit) before drawing. alpha = 0.6 lets overlapping points show through.


Aesthetics set in ggplot() are inherited by every layer — that’s why each species gets its own line. The notes show an extra overall dashed trend line, histogram + density, and log-scaled axes.

Start from the question








Question
Chart
Geometry




Compare a value across categories
Bar chart
geom_bar() / geom_col()


How is one variable distributed?
Histogram, boxplot, violin
geom_histogram(), geom_boxplot()


How are two variables related?
Scatter plot

How does something change over time?

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Bar charts: geom_bar vs geom_col






ImportantTask



Plot (a) the number of penguins of each species, and (b) the mean body mass of each species.




ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species)) +
  geom_bar()







penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = mean_mass)) +
  geom_col()










geom_bar() counts rows for you. geom_col() draws heights you have already computed.



geom_bar(): give it only an x. It uses stat = "count", so the bar height is the number of rows in each category. Raw data, one row per penguin.
geom_col(): give it an x and a y. It uses stat = "identity", so the bar height is exactly the y value. Summarised data, one row per bar.
Common errors to demo: geom_bar() with a y fails (“must only have an x or y aesthetic”); geom_col() without a y fails (“requires the following missing aesthetics: y”).
geom_bar(stat = "identity") is the same as geom_col(); students will see it in older code online.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Distributions






ImportantTask



Compare the distribution of body mass across species.




ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15) +
  theme_minimal()










The boxplot gives the median and quartiles; the violin shows the shape the boxplot hides (e.g. two peaks).


Build it in two steps: boxplot alone first, then add the violin underneath. Layer order matters — later layers are drawn on top.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Change over time






ImportantTask



Using gapminder, plot life expectancy over time for the UK, Japan and South Korea.




library(gapminder)
gapminder |>
  filter(country %in% c("United Kingdom", "Japan", "Korea, Rep.")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = lifeExp, colour = country)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal()










Lines join points in order, so trends and crossovers stand out — Japan overtakes the UK in the late 1960s, and South Korea almost catches up by 2007.


Good moment to connect back: filter() from week 4 feeding straight into ggplot(). South Korea is "Korea, Rep." in gapminder — a reminder to check how values are spelled in the data before filtering on them.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
ggplot2 won’t stop you


The \(y\)-axis starts at 94,000,000 — a small change looks like an explosion.




US military strategy in Afghanistan, 2009. The New York Times headline: “We Have Met the Enemy, and He Is PowerPoint”. Clutter defeats the message.

section: Which encoding is easiest to read?
text:
Which encoding is easiest to read?






ImportantTask



Rank the five groups from largest to smallest.























Take a vote on the pie first, then reveal the bar chart. Same data; the pie is literally a stacked bar in polar coordinates (coord_polar) — a nice demonstration of the coordinate component of the grammar.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Cleveland & McGill (1984)
How accurately do people judge…


position along a common scale — most accurate




length, then angle and slope




area, volume, colour saturation — least accurate



Put the comparison that matters most on the most accurate encoding. That’s why bar charts usually beat pie charts.

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
Colour blindness






ImportantTask



Around 8% of men and 0.5% of women are colour blind, most often red–green. Make this plot readable for them.



ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g,
                     colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Adelie = "red", Chinstrap = "green",
                                 Gentoo = "blue")) +
  theme_minimal()










ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g,
                     colour = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_brewer(type = "qual") +
  theme_minimal()










Use a colourblind-safe palette (viridis, ColorBrewer) and a redundant encoding like shape, so the plot survives greyscale printing too.


Without type = "qual", scale_colour_brewer() gives a sequential blue palette — ask the room why that would be wrong for species (it implies an order that doesn’t exist).

title: Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
A checklist for every plot


Honest scales — bar charts start at zero




Accurate encodings — key comparison on position or length




No clutter — every element earns its place; use alpha for overplotting




Clear labels — title, axis names, units




Accessible — safe palettes plus redundant encodings



If time allows, go back to the welfare chart and have them critique it against the list — it fails 1, and arguably 4.

text:

build a plot layer by layer: ggplot() + aes() + geom_*() + labs()




pick a chart for the question — bar, distribution, scatter, line — and know geom_bar from geom_col




critique plots for honesty, perceptual accuracy and accessibility

section: One Import is All You Need
text:
One Import is All You Need

library(tidyverse)   # readr + dplyr + tidyr + ggplot2 + ...

Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 4.4.3



The tidyverse is a bundle of packages that share a design philosophy. Loading it gives us readr (loading), dplyr (transforming) and tidyr (reshaping) all at once.


Point out the startup message: it lists the attached packages and flags any conflicts (e.g. dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()). This is normal. Contrast with library(dplyr) alone from last week — today we want the whole toolkit.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Reading a CSV






ImportantTask



Load data/penguins.csv and take a look. What type of object comes back?




penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")
penguins

# A tibble: 344 × 9
   rowid species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm
   <dbl> <chr>   <chr>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <dbl>
 1     1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181
 2     2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186
 3     3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195
 4     4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA
 5     5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193
 6     6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190
 7     7 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181
 8     8 Adelie  Torgersen           39.2          19.6               195
 9     9 Adelie  Torgersen           34.1          18.1               193
10    10 Adelie  Torgersen           42            20.2               190
# ℹ 334 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: body_mass_g <dbl>, sex <chr>, year <dbl>




CSV = Comma Separated Values: plain text, columns split by ,, rows split by a newline. read_csv() returns a tibble — a modern data frame with nicer printing.


Open penguins.csv in a text editor first so they see the commas and the header row. Note the column-type spec read_csv prints — it guessed <dbl>, <chr> etc. for us. Emphasise: the printout tells you the dimensions and the type of every column.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
Other delimiters






ImportantTask



The file data/penguins_pipe.txt holds the same data, but columns are separated by | instead of ,. Try read_csv() on it — then load it properly.




read_delim("data/penguins_pipe.txt", delim = "|")

# A tibble: 344 × 9
   rowid species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm
   <dbl> <chr>   <chr>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <dbl>
 1     1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181
 2     2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186
 3     3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195
 4     4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA
 5     5 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193
 6     6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190
 7     7 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181
 8     8 Adelie  Torgersen           39.2          19.6               195
 9     9 Adelie  Torgersen           34.1          18.1               193
10    10 Adelie  Torgersen           42            20.2               190
# ℹ 334 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: body_mass_g <dbl>, sex <chr>, year <dbl>




read_csv() is just read_delim() with delim = ",". For any other delimiter (tabs → read_tsv(), or anything via read_delim(delim = ...)) you pick the matching reader.


First do read_csv("data/penguins_pipe.txt") and let it fail / mangle — everything lands in one column. The lesson: look at the file (open it) to find the delimiter, then choose the reader. Mention that if you don’t know the format you experiment until it loads.

title: Data Wrangling in R
text:
The five verbs
dplyr gives us a small set of readable verbs:


mutate() — add or change columns
select() — pick columns
filter() — pick rows
arrange() — reorder rows
summarise() — collapse many rows to a summary




We’ll demo them on gapminder: country-level life expectancy, population and GDP per capita over time.



library(gapminder)
gapminder

# A tibble: 1,704 × 6
   country     continent  year lifeExp      pop gdpPercap
   <fct>       <fct>     <int>   <dbl>    <int>     <dbl>

 2 Afghanistan Asia       1957    30.3  9240934      821.
 3 Afghanistan Asia       1962    32.0 10267083      853.
 4 Afghanistan Asia       1967    34.0 11537966      836.
 5 Afghanistan Asia       1972    36.1 13079460      740.
 6 Afghanistan Asia       1977    38.4 14880372      786.
 7 Afghanistan Asia       1982    39.9 12881816      978.
 8 Afghanistan Asia       1987    40.8 13867957      852.
 9 Afghanistan Asia       1992    41.7 16317921      649.

ImportantTask



Write clip(x, lower, upper) that forces a value into a range — e.g. for cleaning impossible measurements.

What is “Literate Programming”?
Literate programming is a methodology introduced by Donald Knuth, whereby:

Explanations are written alongside code
The document can be “rendered” (“knitted”) to produce a readable report.
Changes in code are automatically reflected in the output to reduce manual mistakes.

Frameworks like Quarto implement Literate programming.

Objectives

text:
Packages

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Why not one big table?


Size: a flat table repeats every student’s name for every course




Integrity: a name change is made in one place




Flexibility: new tables (e.g. references) can link to students without touching grades




Clarity: the structure mirrors the real world — “each student takes many courses”



Keep this short — the point is that real data arrives split up on purpose, so joining is a routine step, not a workaround. The SQL week will return to this idea.

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Clean the column names first






Task


Column names like Date of Birth need backticks every time. Fix this for both tables.





student_data <- clean_names(student_data)
student_grades <- clean_names(student_grades)
names(student_data)

[1] "id"            "given_name"    "family_name"   "date_of_birth"

names(student_grades)

[1] "student_id" "course"     "grade"     




clean_names() converts everything to snake_case. Make it a habit when loading messy data.

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Where did the rows go?






Task


Compare the number of rows in joined and student_grades. Which students have been lost, and why?





nrow(joined)

[1] 53

nrow(student_grades)

[1] 59

setdiff(student_grades$student_id, student_data$id)  # grades, no student

[1] 21 22

setdiff(student_data$id, joined$id)                  # student, no grades

[1] 7




An inner join keeps only rows with a match in both tables.


Students 21 and 22 have grades but no student record; student 7 has no grades at all. anti_join(student_data, student_grades, by = ...) answers the same question and returns the full rows — it’s in the notes.

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Two common surprises






Duplicated column names


If both tables have a non-key column with the same name (say notes), you get notes.x and notes.y. Control this with the suffix argument.









Many-to-many joins


If both tables have several rows per key, you get every combination — the row count can explode. dplyr warns you; it is usually a mistake.




Rule of thumb: check nrow() before and after every join.

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
stringr
Every function starts str_ and is vectorised: it works on one string or a whole column.

str_length(c("Alice", "Bob", "Dave"))

[1] 5 3 4



Free text from forms is rarely clean:

messy_names <- c("  Alice  ", "BOB", "cara-mae", "  dave ")

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Case and whitespace






Task


Remove the stray spaces from messy_names and give them consistent capitalisation.





str_trim(messy_names)

[1] "Alice"    "BOB"      "cara-mae" "dave"    

str_squish("  too    many   spaces ")

[1] "too many spaces"

str_to_title(str_squish(messy_names))

[1] "Alice"    "Bob"      "Cara-Mae" "Dave"    




str_trim() removes spaces at the ends; str_squish() also collapses runs inside. Case: str_to_lower(), str_to_upper(), str_to_title().

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Detecting patterns






Task


Which names contain an "a"? Why isn’t "Alice" one of them?





str_detect(messy_names, "a")

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE

str_detect(str_to_lower(messy_names), "a")

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE




Matching is case-sensitive — standardise case first. str_detect() returns TRUE/FALSE, so it drops straight into filter().

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Replacing and removing






Task


Turn "cara-mae" into "cara mae", and get just the number from "MATH6195".





str_replace("cara-mae", "-", " ")

[1] "cara mae"

str_replace_all("a-b-c-d", "-", "_")

[1] "a_b_c_d"

str_remove("MATH6195", "MATH")

[1] "6195"




str_replace() changes the first match; str_replace_all() changes every match.

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
In a pipeline






Task


Clean a whole column of names inside mutate().





tibble(raw = messy_names) |>
  mutate(clean = str_to_title(str_squish(raw)))

# A tibble: 4 × 2
  raw         clean   
  <chr>       <chr>   
1 "  Alice  " Alice   
2 "BOB"       Bob     
3 "cara-mae"  Cara-Mae
4 "  dave "   Dave    









Regular expressions


Patterns are regular expressions: ., * and ? have special meanings. Not examined, but worth learning — try regex101.

title: Joins, Strings and Dates
text:
Dates are ambiguous
Is 08/11/2025 11 August or 8 November?






Task


Parse "2025-August-11", "11/08/25" and "8.11.2025" as the same date.





d1 <- ymd("2025-August-11")
d2 <- dmy("11/08/25")
d3 <- mdy("8.11.2025")
c(d1, d2, d3)

text:
Two common surprises






WarningDuplicated column names



If both tables have a non-key column with the same name (say notes), you get notes.x and notes.y. Control this with the suffix argument.








WarningMany-to-many joins



If both tables have several rows per key, you get every combination — the row count can explode. dplyr warns you; it is usually a mistake.



Rule of thumb: check nrow() before and after every join.
